scenes.tts: This is the T cell receptor. It tells a T cell that it has found an infected cell. But inside the cell, its tail is only a few amino acids long. It holds no enzyme anywhere, not even a kinase. So how does it send a message?
scenes.visual: A receptor spans the T-cell membrane and touches a peptide on an MHC protein of another cell; its stub of a tail inside points down to a crossed-out enzyme chip and a dashed question-mark box.
scenes.narration: This is the T cell receptor. It tells a T cell that it has found an infected cell. But inside the cell, its tail is only a few amino acids long. It holds no enzyme anywhere, not even a kinase. So how does it send a message?

scenes.tts: The alpha and beta chains do the recognising. Beside them sit partner chains, called C D 3 and zeta. Their tails reach into the cell. Each tail carries a short motif of two tyrosines, a fixed short distance apart. This motif is called an I T A M.
scenes.caption: The alpha and beta chains do the recognising. Beside them sit partner chains, called CD3 and zeta. Their tails reach into the cell. Each tail carries a short motif of two tyrosines, a fixed short distance apart. This motif is called an ITAM.
scenes.visual: Partner chains grow beside the receptor and their long tails grow down into the cell; two tyrosine dots appear on each tail and a frame around each pair is labelled ITAM.
scenes.narration: The alpha and beta chains do the recognising. Beside them sit partner chains, called CD3 and zeta. Their tails reach into the cell. Each tail carries a short motif of two tyrosines, a fixed short distance apart. This motif is called an ITAM.

scenes.tts: So where is the kinase? It is borrowed from a neighbour. A co-receptor, C D 4 or C D 8, grips the display protein M H C that the receptor reads. A share of the tyrosine kinase L C K rides on its inner tail, beside the partner tails. L C K then adds a phosphate to both tyrosines.
scenes.caption: So where is the kinase? It is borrowed from a neighbour. A co-receptor, CD4 or CD8, grips the display protein MHC that the receptor reads. A share of the tyrosine kinase Lck rides on its inner tail, beside the partner tails. Lck then adds a phosphate to both tyrosines.
scenes.visual: A dashed kinase question box becomes Lck on a co-receptor that hooks onto the MHC protein; Lck slides beside a partner tail, the view zooms to that one tail, and two phosphate badges land on its two tyrosines.
scenes.narration: So where is the kinase? It is borrowed from a neighbour. A co-receptor, CD4 or CD8, grips the display protein MHC that the receptor reads. A share of the tyrosine kinase Lck rides on its inner tail, beside the partner tails. Lck then adds a phosphate to both tyrosines.

scenes.tts: Now the reader arrives: zap seventy, a second kinase. It has two S H two domains, side by side. Each domain grips one phosphotyrosine, and the pair is spaced to fit the two on one tail. With one phosphate, it binds weakly. It binds tightly only when both tyrosines carry a phosphate, so one stray phosphate does not start a T cell.
scenes.caption: Now the reader arrives: ZAP-70, a second kinase. It has two SH2 domains, side by side. Each domain grips one phosphotyrosine, and the pair is spaced to fit the two on one tail. With one phosphate, it binds weakly. It binds tightly only when both tyrosines carry a phosphate, so one stray phosphate does not start a T cell.
scenes.visual: ZAP-70 drops onto the tail with two open cups spaced like the two tyrosines; with one phosphate only one cup closes and the protein wobbles, with both phosphates both cups close tight.
scenes.narration: Now the reader arrives: ZAP-70, a second kinase. It has two SH2 domains, side by side. Each domain grips one phosphotyrosine, and the pair is spaced to fit the two on one tail. scenes.tts: Docking opens zap seventy, which phosphorylates L A T, a scaffold set in the membrane. From L A T, one branch raises calcium, and N F A T enters the nucleus. A second runs through D A G and protein kinase C to N F kappa B. A third loads Ras, and E R K helps build A P one. The three meet on genes such as the one for interleukin two.
scenes.caption: Docking opens ZAP-70, which phosphorylates LAT, a scaffold set in the membrane. From LAT, one branch raises calcium, and NFAT enters the nucleus. A second runs through DAG and protein kinase C to NF-κB. A third loads Ras, and ERK helps build AP-1. The three meet on genes such as the one for interleukin-2.
scenes.visual: ZAP-70 turns on and shrinks aside; a phosphate passes to the LAT bar, then three rows grow out of LAT, each ending at a transcription-factor chip, and the three chips point at one gene bar.
scenes.narration: Docking opens ZAP-70, which phosphorylates LAT, a scaffold set in the membrane. From LAT, one branch raises calcium, and NFAT enters the nucleus. A second runs through DAG and protein kinase C to NF-κB. A third loads Ras, and ERK helps build AP-1. The three meet on genes such as the one for interleukin-2.

scenes.tts: Even this is not enough, because receptors vary almost at random, and some fit the body's own peptides. In classic experiments on cultured T cells, signal one alone did worse than nothing. The cells entered a lasting unresponsive state called anergy. A second signal needs the receptor C D 28 to bind a B 7 protein on the presenting cell. Keep the rule: a T cell needs two phosphates and two signals.
